# Changes Since Deliverable 3

>I have altered my final charts to include all of their original variables rather than only a select few. I now realize that I must consider all the data at my disposal to locate any possible relationships among properties, rather than just focusing on the variables that are the most relevent. As a result, the entire "Selection of Variables" portion from the Data Organization portion of my work from Deliverable 3 has been removed. My processing plan has also been altered to reflect this change, making it much shorter.

>While double-checking my data, I noticed that the total amount of values in IOLPL and the leased properties mentioned in IOLPB do not match. Upon further research into the true nature of the IOLP, I have learned that the Leased properties data subset in my original data refers to the individual lease contracts instead of the properties themselves. To maintain consistancy, I am altering my data to only include the data from IOLPB, which focuses on the properties themselves, giving me a better idea of the distribution of government infrastructure. many of the later mentions of IOLPL have been altered, and my data cleaning plan disregards it. It is still mentioned in the initial overview and descriptions of my data for the sake of providing a complete overview of the raw data.

>In my summary statistics, I altered my charts of property distribution among states and GSA regions to be single histograms that show all the obesrvations, differentiated by color. I also altered the names and titles in the table displaying property distribution among cities.


# Mission Statement
 
>My ultimate goal for my project is to determine wether or not any patterns exist within the distribution of leased or owned Government Properties within the United States. However, doing so requires the IOLP data to be refined into a more compact state. The following markdown outlines the preprocessing of said data.

# Data Organization & Observations
## Section 1: Presentation of Raw Data
### Overview of Raw Data

>The following block of code contains a preview of the raw data tables I have chosen for my project. While there was also a second data frames containing the dates of each property's lease, I am mainly focusing on property distribution. Therefore, I only require the first dataset, which contains every property, leased and owned. I have titled this set of data "IOLPB," which is short for IOLP Buildings. The second data frames only contains leased properties, and has been named "IOLPL," short for IOLP Leases.

```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
IOLPB<-read.csv("IOLPBuildings.csv")
head(IOLPB,10)
IOLPL<-read.csv("IOLPLeases.csv")
head(IOLPL,10)
```

### Chart Dimensions

>IOLPB: 7,758 observations, 18 variables

>IOLPL: 7,074 observations, 19 variables


### Data Dictionary

>The following "data dictionary" serves as an overview of each variable in the data, and provides the following:

>1. The variable's name.
2. A brief description of the variable and its contents.
3. Which of the two data-sets the variable is in ("IOLPB" or "IOLPL").
4. The data type of the variable (categorical or numerical).

>**NOTE:** Descriptions of the data can also be found on the website that I pulled the data from.

>[Source of data and overview of the variables within it](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/inventory-of-owned-and-leased-properties-iolp)

#### "Location.Code"

>This variable contains location codes, the GSA's method for identifying each property.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable Type: Categorial

#### "Real.Property.Asset.Name"

>This variable contains the name of each property. It was made with the intent of aiding viewers of the data in locating information on specific properties. A handfull of the values within this variable match their observations's entry in the "Street.Address" variable.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable type: Categorical

#### "Installation.Name"

>This variable primarily consists of N/A values. The few values that it does list are meant to group together properties that are parts of specific instilations.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable type: Categorical

#### "Owned.or.Leased"

>This variable seperates leased and owned properties. Its entries are all either "OWNED" or "LEASED." This data will be invaluable for determining the distribution of the two types of property across the United States.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB

>Variable type: Categorical

#### "GSA.Region"

> The GSA, the administration that curates the IOLP and locates property for government use, divides the acuisition and management of various properties among 11 districts, with each one encompassing different states. This variable organizes properties into districts using a number associated with each district.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable type: Functionally categorical, yet displayed as numerical.

#### "Street.Address"

>This variable contains the street adress of the properties in the address. Some of the entries in this variable correspond with their observations's value in the "Real.Property.Asset.Name" variable.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable type: Categorical

> This variable contains the name of the city that each property is located in.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

>Variable type: Categorical

#### "State"

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

> This variable contains each property's zip code.

>This variable is present in: IOLPB, IOLPL

### Raw Data Cleanliness Assessment

>The current state of the data seems somewhat well organized. Every property has a corresponding coordinate grid entry and state, which are the two main variables I had in mind when initially designing my project. However, many of the more specific variables, such as the values within the "Congressional.District.Representatives.Name" and "Instillation.Name" variables seem to primarily consist of N/A values. This makes sense, as not all properties are part of specific instillations.

>Certain variables also seem to contain high levels of repitition. For example, every ovservation of the "Real.Property.Asset.Type" variable is a building, and every property is labled "active" according to the "Building.Status" variable. While variables like this display valid information and have obvious purposes, they will not necisarily help me inderstand the general concentration of properties.

>Thankfully, as my project mainly focuses on the general distribution of the properties within the IOLP, I will not need variables regarding finer details or specific identification.

## Section 2: Filtration of Data
### Processing plan

>While cleaning my data, I will need to remove certain observations from both charts, as some of the properties listed in the IOLP lie outside of the United States, and are therefore irrelevant to my final results. Furthermore,  However, since Washington DC counts as a U.S. territory, I will leave it, as it still lies within the main United States.

> As for the data frames themselves, I will primarily be using IOLPB for future maps, as it contains all the properties. IOLPL concerns includes individual lease agreements, therefore having more entries than the proper amount of leased properties mentioned in IOLPB. IOLPB will be split into three charts; One containing all properties, one containing leased properties, and one containing owned properties. After that, I can simplify the data into as many smaller tables as I deem nessecary to properly compare data.

### Code
####Removal of Territories

>The following code removes US territories from IOLPB and IOLPL, saving them as new data frames labled IOLPBUS and IOLPLUS respectively. This is accomplished by using the filter function selecting values within the state column that are not equal to US territories, except for Washington DC.

>**NOTE**The territories being removed are American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and the US Virgin Islands. This is 5 territories in total.

```{r}
IOLPBUS<-IOLPB%>%filter(State!="AS"&State!="GU"&State!="MP"&State!="PR"&State!="VI"&State!="CU")
```

#### Final Seperation and Naming of Data Frames

>The last thing I plan to do in the processing of my data is to create one final data frame from IOLPBUSR that contains only the owned properties, then rename each data frame to a more suitable name, ultimately giving me one data frame that contains all the properties, and two data frames that only contain leased or owned properties. This will allow for maximum ease in sorting through the values.

```{r}
IOLP.all<-IOLPBUS
IOLP.owned<-(IOLPBUS%>%filter(Owned.or.Leased=="OWNED")%>%select(-Owned.or.Leased))
IOLP.leased<-(IOLPBUS%>%filter(Owned.or.Leased=="LEASED")%>%select(-Owned.or.Leased))
head(IOLP.all,10)
head(IOLP.owned,10)
head(IOLP.leased,10)
```


### Final Chart Dimensions

IOLP.all: 7,659 observations, 18 variables
IOLP.leased: 5,989 observations, 17 variables
IOLP.owned: 1,670 observations, 17 variables

## Section 3: Observations of Refined Data
### Summary Statistics
####Property Distribution Among States

>The following chart displays the distributions of properties among states, both owned and leased. Due to the odd formatting that resulted from the quantity of states, the charts have been made interactive for easier viewing.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
options(scipen = 999)
statesbar.all<-IOLP.all%>%group_by(State)%>%summarise(Property.Density=n())%>%arrange(-Property.Density)%>%mutate(state = State)
                                                   
                                                   

IOLP.all.and.Statesbars<-full_join(IOLP.all, statesbar.all, by = "State") 

propdist<-(ggplot(IOLP.all.and.Statesbars) +
geom_bar(aes(x = State, fill = Owned.or.Leased))+scale_fill_manual(values = c(
"LEASED" = "blue","OWNED" = "orange"))+coord_flip()+labs(x="State", y="Government Properties", title="Total Property Distribution Among States"))

ggplotly(propdist)
                                                   
                                                                                                   
```

####Property Distribution Among Cities

>In the following table, I located the quantity of total properties within certain cities, as well as what percentage of total property is within each city. Due to the large quantity of cities in the IOLP, I have presented the information in a table rather than a graph. Should the distribution of properties among states prove to be too underwhelming, this should allow me to notice whether or not any patterns exist in the distributions of government properties among cities, as larger cities in specific states may possess particularily large amounts of property.

>Unlike the previous graph, I have calculated seperate visuals for total property, owned property, and leased property.

>Due to the very large number of cities within the IOLP, I have arranged them into tables.

```{r}
IOLP.all.city<-IOLP.all%>%group_by(City)%>%summarize(Total.Property.Density=n())%>%arrange(-Total.Property.Density)%>%mutate(precent=(((Total.Property.Density/(sum(Total.Property.Density)))*100)))%>%mutate(percent=round(precent,2))%>%select(City,Total.Property.Density,percent)
head(IOLP.all.city,10)

IOLP.leased.city<-IOLP.leased%>%group_by(City)%>%summarize(Leased.Property.Density=n())%>%arrange(-Leased.Property.Density)%>%mutate(precent=(((Leased.Property.Density/(sum(Leased.Property.Density)))*100)))%>%mutate(percent=round(precent,2))%>%select(City,Leased.Property.Density,percent)
head(IOLP.leased.city,10)

IOLP.owned.city<-IOLP.owned%>%group_by(City)%>%summarize(Owned.Property.Density=n())%>%arrange(-Owned.Property.Density)%>%mutate(precent=(((Owned.Property.Density/(sum(Owned.Property.Density)))*100)))%>%mutate(percent=round(precent,2))%>%select(City,Owned.Property.Density,percent)
head(IOLP.owned.city,10)
```

####Property Distribution Among GSA Regions
>This chart displays the amount of states within each congressional district. This will grant me access to more aspects of the data to compare. I plan to eventually compare the amount of cities within states and GSA districts to the amount of properties within states and GSA districts. Doing so will allow me to see if the GSA regions were chosen for a specific region, such as the amount of properties within them or the amount of cities within them.

```{r}
Distribution.GSA<-IOLP.all%>%group_by(GSA.Region)%>%summarize(Property.Density=n())%>%arrange(-GSA.Region)
IOLP.all.and.GSA<-full_join(IOLP.all, Distribution.GSA, by = "GSA.Region")

ggplotly(ggplot(IOLP.all.and.GSA)+geom_bar(aes(x=GSA.Region,fill=Owned.or.Leased))+scale_fill_manual(values = c(
"LEASED" = "blue","OWNED" = "orange"))+labs(x="GSA Region", y="Properties Within Region", title="GSA Property Distribution Among Its Regions (all)"))
```


# Discussion

>Now that I have properly combed through the data, I have come to truly comprehend its massive scope. The IOLP is intended to organize GSA property, and therefore several variables are included within it, allowing it to answer as many theoretical questions as it possibly can. It is because of this intricacy that I have begun to feel a bit self concious of my project's original scope. However, Many of the variables refer to very specific factors, such as square footage available and the individual in charge of their congressional district. While such variables offer a plethora of intriguing data, they simply aren't relevent to my project's current scope, which is not necessarily a bad thing. If I worry about this too much, I will only 
>as for the variables that are more relevant for my objectives, I can already begin to see noticable trends in them. For example, Washington DC has only the third most total property out of all the states, while it has the most owned property out of all the states. This makes sense, as since DC houses our national capital, it would require the most full-time infrastructure. I also noticed that Texas has the most total property, and California contains the most leased property. While this detail does fascinate me, I will need to construct a map with this data before I am able to tell whether or not this means anything in relation to other states. In a simmilar vein, GSA region 4 has the most total property and leased property, but GSA 12 has the most owned property. This means the assigned number of each GSA region is not coorelated to the quantity of properties within it.

>My next primary goal is still the creation of maps. I plan to use the "Leaflet" package to create maps to display the differences in the distribution of all properties in the IOLP, the leased properties, and the owned properties. However, I will also use the City and GSA region variables to look for further comparisons in the data, and figure out if the size of GSA regions has anything to do with the amount of cities, states, or properties within a certain area. This data will not only open up opportunities for future research, but also theoretically allow the GSA and federal government to look through the density of their properties and decide wether or not they lack or have an excess of infrastructure in specific locations Furthermore, during the creation of these maps, I may have to remove DC from the properties considered in it, as the values associated with DC may be improperly processed during map creation. This shouldn't be too consequential, as I can already the reasoning behind the property distribution in DC. Furthermore, I can still include it in a map displaying scattered points.


# Exploratory Data Visualizations
## Property Distribution Among States

```{r}
ggplotly(propdist)
```

> While this chart has been pulled from my deliverable 3 submission, it does a good job of displaying the proper property distribution across states. Seemingly, DC has the most owned property, while Texas and California have the most total property. While DC's density of owned property is likely due to its status as the capital, I have reason to believe that the density of property in California and Texas may be related to the extensive population of both states, as the two states are the most densely populated in America.

##Property Distribution Among America in Relation to Latitude and Longitude

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
state_counts <- IOLP.all %>%
count(State, name = "properties") %>%
mutate(region = tolower(state.name[match(State, state.abb)]))

state_shape <- map_data("state") %>%
left_join(state_counts, by = "region")

ggplot(state_shape, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = properties)) +
geom_polygon(color = "white") +
coord_map() +
labs(title = "Property Distribution Across America", fill = "Properties")


state_countsB <- IOLP.all %>%
count(State, name = "properties") %>% filter(State!="CA"&State!="TX"&State!="DC")%>%
mutate(region = tolower(state.name[match(State, state.abb)]))

state_shapeB <- map_data("state") %>%
left_join(state_countsB, by = "region")

ggplot(state_shapeB, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = properties)) +
geom_polygon(color = "white") +
coord_map() +
labs(title = "Property Distribution Across America Disregarding Outliers", fill = "Properties")


```
>The map shown is a simple comparison of latitude and longitute in relation to the total property within each state. The first chart shows the total property distribution across the country by state. However, I realized that the appearence of the chart was skewed by the sheer density of property in Texas and California. The second chart shows the concentration of properties in other states, without the gradient being skewed by the presence of Texas or California.

>I created this chart to get an idea of the general distribution of properties. I now see that there is a slight concentration of properties in the Eastern United states, closer to the capital. However, I also believe that the small size, close proximity, and general age of the Eastern States may have something to do with this concentration.

## Correlation Between the Available and Rentable Square Footage of Properties

```{r}

ggplot(IOLP.all, aes(x = Building.Rentable.Square.Feet, y = Available.Square.Feet, color = Owned.or.Leased)) + geom_point(alpha = .3) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + scale_color_manual(values = c("LEASED" = "blue", "OWNED" = "orange")) + 
  labs(x = "Rentable Square Feet", y = "Available Square Feet",
title = "Relationship between Rentable and Available Square Feet (Owned and Leased)",
color = "Ownership")

ggplot(IOLP.all, aes(x = Building.Rentable.Square.Feet, y =Available.Square.Feet )) +
  geom_point(alpha=.3)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color="black") + scale_color_manual(values = c("LEASED" = "blue", "OWNED" = "orange"))+
  labs(x = "Rentable Square Feet", y = "Available Square Feet",
       title = "Relationship between Rentable and Available Square Feet (Total)")

cor(IOLP.all$Building.Rentable.Square.Feet, IOLP.all$Available.Square.Feet,use = "complete.obs")
cor(IOLP.leased$Building.Rentable.Square.Feet, IOLP.leased$Available.Square.Feet,use = "complete.obs")
cor(IOLP.owned$Building.Rentable.Square.Feet, IOLP.owned$Available.Square.Feet,use = "complete.obs")

Square.Footage.Coorelations<-data.frame(Owned.or.Leased=c("Both Property Types", "Leased Property Only", "Owned Property Only"), r.value=c(0.3711299, 0.3746012, 0.5668776))

Square.Footage.Coorelations
```
> I created this chart to check if there was any correlation between the available and rentable square footage of the properties within the IOLP. Said correlation could theoretically show if government buildings have any kind of standard size. While there is a correlation of about 0.37 among the total properties, which indicates moderate correlation, there simply isn't enough data in the data set to imply that either variable has a signifigant impact on the GSA's choice of properties. Furthermore, not every property in the IOLP had an actual value in either one of the square footage columns, further discrediting this chart's potential causation.

> However, I have noticed that the leased properties, despite being higher in quantity, seem to be much more concentrated at zero available and rentable square feet. Meanwhile, the available and rentable square footage of the owned properties tends to be much higher and spread out.

> Another odd detail is that the leased property has a slightly higher r value by a few thousandths, and the owned property has a much larger r value, being larger than both by roughly 0.2. I believe that the higher trend in the owned property may indicate my previously mentoined hypothesis of certain government properties following specific trends or guidelines, but this information alone does not ensure causation.

> As for the linear trend lines, it seems that there is a much steeper trend line among the leased properties. I am not sure if there is any signifigance behind this.

> While there seems to be a handfull of trends in this relationship, I sadly lack enough information and knowledge to make any more solid conclusions from them.

## Histogram of Available and Rentable Square Footage

```{r}
ggplot(IOLP.all)+geom_histogram(aes(x = Available.Square.Feet,),fill="green") + labs(x= "Available Square Footage", y="Properties")

ggplot(IOLP.all)+geom_histogram(aes(x = Building.Rentable.Square.Feet),fill="red")+labs(x="Rentable Square Footage", y="Properties")
```
> These are simple histograms showing the comparison between the square footage of total properties. Strangely, it seems that they both follow a simmilar pattern, with many of the properties having no rentable or available square footage. However, upon seeing these graphs, I now understand that this lack of rentable or vacant property more likely reflects the efficiant use of government properties, as there is very little property being rented commercially or marked as "vacant".

## Map (Individual Properties)
```{r}
state_shape <- map_data("state")

ggplot() +
geom_polygon(data = state_shape, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
fill = "grey85", color = "white") +
geom_point(data = filter(IOLP.leased, State != "AK" & State != "HI"),
aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = "Leased")) +
geom_point(data = filter(IOLP.owned, State != "AK" & State != "HI"),
aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, color = "Owned")) +
scale_color_manual(values = c("Leased" = "blue", "Owned" = "orange")) +
coord_map() +
labs(title = "Owned and Leased Property Distribution",
x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Property Type")
```
>This map displays the data my project was initially created for; The distribution of property across the United States, arranged by latitude and longitude, as well as differentiated between owned and leased property.

>While both this map and the previous map show a noticable density of property near the Eastern United States, this map allowed me to notice another pattern; A noticable concentration of owned properties located near the Northern and Southern borders of the country. This makes perfect sense, as the government would need to keep a constant watch over the border to properly manage immigration and security.

>Furthermore, the previously mentioned density in the Eastern United States seems to be moreso due on the small size and close proximity of the eastern states. In reality, the placement and age of these states likely does not matter as much as I originally expected.




# Overall Take

> Upon looking at the scatterpoint maps, I now believe that I properly understand the distribution of properties in the IOLP. While the total property appears to be more dense in the Eastern states, that is partially due to the small size and proximity of those states. The property of the states themselves may be connected to population, as a quick search revealed that Texas and California, the two states with the most total property, also posess the highest populations out of all the states. The scatterplot map of the properties also allowed me to notice that numerous government-onwed properties seem to be housed on the country's Northern and Southern borders, likely to allow better control over our interactions with neighboring countries.

> Sadly, my results in locating any other kind of pattern in the data more or less fell short. Although I was able to locate some level of correlation between the available and rentable square footage of each property using the histogram and scatterplot chart, I was only able to form a conclusion that each value tended to minimize the vacant and unused space. While this means that the government is likely being efficient with the usage of these properties, it simply isn't the kind of massive takeaway I had previously envisioned. The map that compared the states based on population via shading was also slightly underwhelming. The states to the east did have a slightly more noticeable density in property, but said density was not quite as big as I had excpected, and was overshadowed by the sheer amount of properties in Texas and California, further supporting the idea that population may be connected to the amount of government properties in each state.

> Ultimately, this deliverable has simply taught me how limited in scope my original idea was. While I did manage to identify trends in property placement as I had originally sought to do, I have also gained the understanding of how limited the scope of my chosen data set is. While the IOLP does posess many variables for each observation, many of them are purely categorical, such as the State or GSA region they reside in. Going into the project, I understood that the IOLP was made to allow others to view owned and leased government properties, but I now understand that this severely limits its informative quality. To properly confirm any of my conclusions, such as the relationship between property density and population among states or the efficient use of government property, I would have to do outside research and take other data sets into consideration. I origionally chose this data set because I simply thought it would be enough to locate noteworthy details from a set of data. However, this initial lack of a well defined goal alongside a large and somewhat odd set of raw data has left me feeling insecure and dissatisfied with my analysis. For my final draft, I plan to focus on the few details and conclusions I have located and formulated regarding property placement across the central American states, and locate outside statistics to back them up. Despite the IOLP's now glaring limitations, I still believe that I have located somewhat relevant or usable data that will help me form a decent final draft and presentation.
